He did not realize he had lost his fundamental essence;
though he strove diligently, the day he would return to the source had not yet arrived.
Therefore, relying on principle and based upon the teachings,
I have briefly composed this "Discourse on the Platter" (Pan-shi),
hoping that those who cling to mere names [will be enlightened].
One returns to the nameless, true source.
Regarding the method of reading poetry,
one should begin with the Middle Way (Zhongfa).
Winding and meandering in various turns until reaching the Buddha as the conclusion;
read along the path of the seals.
Death and nirvana are eternally in harmony; therefore, the realm is truly a precious palace.

Exhausting all seated thoughts, one gives rise to the principle that emerges from the profusion of phenomena. Beneficial conduct accords with the Dharma-intent, which is like grasping at skillful reality.
Awakening does not exist within the objects of the human realm; for those who seek benefit, the provisions for the journey are adorned by the excellence of the ultimate limit.
Right reflection can bring back those who are deeply obscured; by means of conditions within the mundane, one may then deliberate upon the sages.
Thus, the three types of vessels are fundamentally precious, following the lotus-like purity;
when the Way is not present, the rain falls universally like the ocean seal, reaching all limits until the end, whereupon one attains the Ni-lo (Aniruddha) bed.
The Jewel of Mind; the ten distinct divisions of the Buddha; arising from the cessation of false certainties;
certainly not old; generating and increasing; filling the void; the assembly of all dharmas; the Buddha as the name; movement without coming;
initial accomplishment; distinct separation; chaotic mixture; non-nature; other realms; wondrous; not guarding the self.
Within every atom throughout the ten directions, there is still fullness yet not true minuteness;

nameless in nature, it contains thought as it arises, and that single thought is likewise fused. Knowing that the nature is ultimate and phenomena are non-existent, within this middle way, eons are identical to the one mark of suchness.
This mark is non-referential, profoundly deep, utterly tranquil, and beyond conditions.
Dust has no distant measure; there is neither "is" nor "mutual. The two wisdoms realize all things;
the once-returner accomplishes minute measure. The nine and ten worlds are the characteristics of all phenomena;
they are unmoving from their original state. One is one, yet it is all; one is one, yet within it is all. Within one is all.
The *Diagram of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle* extends to two hundred and ten characters.
The *Great Record* states:
"These diagrams of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle and others are allocated to Master Yuanyan’s fivefold Sea-Seal."

It is said that the "Single Vehicle" (Ekayāna) and the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) correspond to the "Ocean-Seal of Forgotten Images. The commentary on the first fascicle states: "This is the correspondence for the explanation.
The single character 'tu' (圖) corresponds to the 'Ocean-Seal of Manifested Images.
This is because 'tu' means 'image' (xiàng)."
The Sūtra says:
"He immediately manifests supernatural powers just like that image.
The Master of the Tripiṭaka (Kuiji) explains:
Just as they have contemplated,
regarding the one hundred and twenty-four questions above and all the Dharma-gates taught down to the sixth assembly,
those who answer these questions do so with complete clarity and perfection within the Tathāgata’s body of the Dharma-realm.
"...its image manifests instantaneously," and so forth.
The subsequent scripture states:
"Within the pure *dharmakāya*..."
"Because it is formless and does not manifest.
The above passage applies to both internal realization and external transformation;
here, it is applied specifically to internal realization.
The combination of the verse and the seal corresponds to the Buddha’s outward-facing ocean-seal (sāgaramudrā).
That is to say, the verse represents the faculty of Samantabhadra,
while the seal represents the Buddha’s outward-directed mind.
This is because the Buddha’s outward-facing mind-seal is in profound accord with the inward-facing mind of Samantabhadra’s great capacity.
The fifty-four corners correspond to Samantabhadra entering meditative concentration to contemplate the ocean seal.
This refers to two meanings regarding Samantabhadra’s internal realization.
First, if one considers the gate of the Buddha-Samantabhadra,
then Samantabhadra’s entry into meditative concentration is not merely a matter of ultimate realization.
The outward-facing mind-seal also universally realizes the first two ocean-seals;
for when Samantabhadra turns inward, he is the ten Buddhas,
and when the ten Buddhas turn outward, they are Samantabhadra.
Second, if categorized according to the capacities of sentient beings,
[the Śrāvakas] turn away from the Buddha and realize only one portion because they have not yet reached fulfillment; here,
however, we rely on the latter meaning.

Within this Samādhi of the Pure Treasury, the five teachings, up to the infinite capacities of the various vehicles, as well as the "heads and horns" of all phenomena within the Dharma-realm, suddenly manifest.
Two hundred and ten characters correspond to Samantabhadra emerging from samādhi, abiding within the mind and manifesting the ocean-seal of speech.

This refers to the fact that within this "Ocean-Seal" (Sāgaramudrā) [Samādhi], the various dharmas— such as the five cycles of cause and effect— are manifested and established through written characters and verbal expressions.
Such is the intention of Shenlin regarding the *Diagram of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle* (Ekayāna Dharmadhātu Chart).
The phenomena of the dharma-realm are that which is realized;
today my mind is that which realizes.
Thus, this subject and object are both unattainable.
The locus is the vehicle (*yāna*), which is the name for the stage of practice of a single person who cultivates;
because such an immovable rule and boundary are established,
it is called the *dharmadhātu*.
The fundamental locus of the dharmadhātu is this five-foot body of mine.
To demonstrate this meaning, I have depicted it as an image of the entire dharmadhātu as a single body; therefore, it is called a "diagram" (tú).
This means that the central circle within the diagram represents the Three Vehicles.
It signifies that the back of the One Vehicle is the non-abiding fundamental substance within the teachings of the Way;
it is the state where a single thought does not arise, the place of non-duality.
This is because they are attached even to a single characteristic or a single trace in order to receive the fruit of Buddhahood.
"To turn back" refers to the Hīnayāna;
it means not knowing that all phenomena are empty and that suchness is true.
It is simply because they have turned back from attachment to the principle of the emptiness of persons.
Those who are "defeated" are humans and devas;
that is to say, they do not know of the existence of supramundane practice and virtue.
Because those who adhere to the five precepts and the eight precepts perform the karma of humans and devas, they are "crooked";
"crookedness" refers to the three miserable realms.
This means that they do not know the karmic practices for attaining the states of humans and devas.
Because those who stubbornly cling to false views fall into the three miserable realms,
this painting exhaustively depicts the characteristics of the three vehicles and the three miserable realms; thus,
it is said that the image of the single body of the entire dharma-realm is painted.
The Record of the Venerable Dharmarāja states:
"The Diagram of the Dharma-realm of the One Vehicle has two levels of selection.
First, it selects from the division of teaching and takes only the division of realization."
This means that while the Dharma of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) applies to both realization and teaching, the term "realm" (*dhātu*) is used here to distinguish it from the category of teaching.
This is because the category of realization represents the ultimate limit of the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
The second [“one”] serves solely to exclude the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and universally includes both the realization and the teaching aspects of the one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is because the one vehicle is distinguished from the three vehicles;
thus, this “one” of the one vehicle, as well as the “one” that is free from beginning and end (the red seal below), [are so designated].
The "Single-Character Seal" (Iji-in) in the section concerning the mutual origination of the beginning and end with Master Yen is identical in meaning to this.

At the head of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the Single-Character Seal is pressed because it is intended to clarify that throughout the beginning and end of this entire work, every word and every phrase manifests only this One.
Furthermore, regarding the passage in the five-fascicle commentary where it presses the "single-character seal" at the point where the false is shown to be the correct:
if one gives rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena, that is false;
to know that phenomena are one is the correct [view].
This means that if a bodhisattva gives rise to a single thought of anger,
then sixty gates of universal practice will result in one million obstacles.
This is because the mind of anger arises from within the dualistic grasping of self and other.
It is said that if one gives rise to dualistic interpretations, this is precisely error.
If a bodhisattva arouses the great compassion of sameness (samatā-mahākaruṇā),
then the hundred thousand gates of hindrance become the sixty universal practices (pāramitās).
This means that one perceives the phenomena of the three worlds as being one's own body and mind;
because of this, one gives rise to great compassion based on the identity of essence.
Thus, it is said that knowing all phenomena to be one is precisely what constitutes correctness.
Furthermore, regarding the "Single-Syllable Seal" as extracted from the *Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*:
if one perceives all phenomena as dual or triple,
one immediately commits the eight root transgressions.
One cannot enter the dharma-realm of the One Vehicle;
for if one does not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena,
one will immediately attain entry into the dharma-realm of the One Vehicle.
It is the same here: from beginning to end, it does not express two or three,
but merely manifests one.
Regarding what is called "one":
within that which is devoid of subject and object, we provisionally and forcibly differentiate it,
such that there is a "one" as the observing subject and a "one" as the observed object.
That is to say, if one realizes that one's own body and mind encompass all phenomena without partiality or omission, transcending both subject and object,
then this constitutes the capacity for the single contemplation.
This very dwelling place of body and mind is the first object of observation.
Question: Within this oneness, how does one enter?
Answer: This refers to the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Question: What are śamatha and vipaśyanā?
Answer: If one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna):
Sealing the ten universal dharmas with the seal of the six characteristics, such that each stage remains unmoved while merging into one—this vivid clarity is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
It is like a seal impressing an object: it neither lifts nor turns.
When such contemplative wisdom accords with the Dharma, being free from subject and object, utterly non-conceptual and unwavering, this is *śamatha* (calm abiding).
As for "vehicle" (*yāna*), it refers to the ability to maintain decisive faith in that aforementioned single point; thus it is called a vehicle.
Such faith as this is not called a "vehicle" (yāna).
If one speaks of the three vehicles, it is because those who hear the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) cannot believe it instantaneously;
they must believe it through gradual stages.
There are ten levels of faith;
because one cannot understand them instantaneously,
they are understood gradually and sequentially.
There are ten levels of understanding.
Because one cannot realize them instantaneously, but rather realizes them gradually, [the stages] continue up to that point.
There are ten proofs;
because one thus proceeds gradually to the fruit of Buddhahood,
it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
The meaning is that one who comes by means of the path of reality achieves perfect enlightenment.
If it were the One Vehicle (Ekayāna),
then [the goal] would reside in a single, superior location.
If one gives rise to perfect faith, it is itself perfect realization; therefore, it is called a "vehicle.
That "a single movement is all movements" is precisely this meaning.
As for "Dharma," it refers to my own body and mind.
"Dhātu" (realm) refers to this body and mind, which encompass all things, are beyond all relative distinctions, and are severed from the limits of past and future;
it is the meaning of the ultimate boundary of phenomena (*dharma*).
"Diagram" (*tu*) means an image.
Just as one might draw an image of an elephant and show it to someone who does not know what an elephant is,
so too, because the practitioner does not know that their own body and mind are the Buddha of the Dharmadhātu,
they draw an image of the Buddha of the Dharmadhātu to point it out.
The *Excerpts from the "Entering the Dharma Realm" Chapter* states:
Now, regarding the entry into the Dharma Realm, in accordance with what is appropriate, we shall first eliminate its faults by establishing the boundaries of the dharmas.
For a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment and is advancing toward the Mahāyāna, there are eight fundamental transgressions.
Having utterly consumed all roots of goodness, they fall into the evil realms;
they depart from the place of peace and lose the happiness of humans and devas,
and they likewise lose the bliss of the Mahāyāna realm.
Throughout their lives in this world of five turbidities, they possess residual roots of goodness;
they draw near to spiritual friends and take refuge in the profound Dharma.
They give rise to the unsurpassed mind,
hear the profound Dharma,
and read, recite, receive, and uphold it.
When one recites and explains this to those of inferior intelligence,
others, having heard it, will become startled, doubtful, and terrified,
and will consequently retreat and lose heart regarding the bodhicitta.
To delight in the Śrāvaka-yāna is the first grave offense.
One must simply discern their faculties and understand the sequence of their minds, then teach them according to their progression from the shallow to the profound.
Furthermore, he says to people:
"How can you possibly give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna?
It would be better for you to quickly turn toward the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles and enter into nirvāṇa."
This is the second grave offense.
Furthermore, one says to another person:
"What use is it for you to study the precepts and dignified conduct? You should quickly resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind."
To uphold, recite, and chant Mahāyāna sūtras so that one's actions of body,
speech, and mind become pure and one does not undergo evil retribution—
this is the third grave offense.
Furthermore, he says to people:
"You should not read or recite the sūtras of the śrāvakas;
you should instead suppress the sūtras of the śrāvakas."
Within the teachings of the Śrāvakas, one cannot sever the fetters and afflictions;
you should instead listen to and receive the pure, profound Mahāyāna sūtras,
for these can extinguish evil and give rise to bodhi.
If there are those who faithfully accept it, both parties shall incur the fourth grave offense.
Furthermore, for the sake of seeking profit, one preaches the Mahāyāna Dharma.
To hear it said that one gains profit from the Mahāyāna and yet to harbor hatred, disparagement, contempt,
or envy toward it is the fifth grave offense.
Furthermore, to explain the profound Dharma for the sake of seeking profit is likewise a grave offense.
To claim that one has not heard [the teachings] from others and thus transgresses against the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is the sixth grave offense.
Furthermore, to act as a caṇḍāla;
They seize the belongings of other virtuous bhikṣus as well as the property of the Triple Gem,
bestowing them upon government officials and the great king;
relying on the power of the king and his officials, they treat virtuous bhikṣus with contempt, harboring anger, disdain, and jealousy toward them.
This is the seventh grave offense.
Furthermore, one commits evil deeds by relying on the superior power of being a king or an official.
Furthermore, relying on their wealth and generosity,
they treat virtuous bhikṣus with contempt,
mocking, humiliating, and sowing discord among them.
They preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma;
they abandon the authentic Sūtras and Vinaya,
and establish regulations that contravene the Dharma.
To harbor resentment toward bhikṣus who practice wholesome conduct, meditate, or recite the sūtras;
having harbored such resentment, to increase it—
this is the eighth grave offense.
If one has already committed an offense, one should rely on the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to repent and extinguish that transgression.
A bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment, if they wish to propagate the Great Dharma and benefit themselves and others, [should do so].
First, one is freed from the aforementioned faults;
subsequently, by relying on the Dharma Master of the Ninth Stage,
the Dharma-gate will then accord with the Dharma-realm.
The Record of the Venerable Zhenxiu states:
"First is the meaning of 'no other.
The Three Vehicles speak of the oneness of nature."
The "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) is said to mean "one" as its object-condition (*ālambana*). Regarding this "object-condition of one," it refers,
according to the context, to the Middle Way and Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the "Chapter on Dedication" consisting of one hundred phrases, such as "like the sun," "like the moon," and so forth.
Although these are indeed the *tathatā* (suchness),
they possess the name "sun" and the characteristic of the sun.
The moon is called by the name "moon";
it is not that names and appearances do not exist.
However, this is with reference to the realization of Samantabhadra.
These names and characteristics do not exist;
they are merely employed to lead those who rely on names and characteristics toward the three vehicles.
This is distinguished according to the teachings of Samantabhadra.
Question: Since the Middle Way as it pertains to the "following" is already profound, with reference to what further meaning is it realized by Samantabhadra?
Answer: It is realized through the Middle Way as it pertains to the "following," as well as through "suchness."
Because it relies on the teachings of the Three Vehicles and employs names such as "the sun" and "the characteristics of the sun," it is said to be in accord with the teachings.
This "portion of realization" (pramāṇa-bhāga) is beyond the path of language and thus transcends all names.
Because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, it is free from marks (*nimitta*).
Question: If this is so, what is the difference between this state and the silence of Vimalakīrti?
Answer: Vimalakīrti’s silence was due to the inversion of names and marks.
Only by departing from names and characteristics can one achieve silence.
The silence of the Buddha in the ninth assembly is distinctively profound because it is silence within names and characteristics;
that is to say, without abandoning names and characteristics, one is silent right within them.
It is not like empty space, which is utterly devoid of all things;
this is merely a distinction made from the perspective of Samantabhadra’s realization.
Question: It is also extremely profound that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Furthermore, by what meaning is this established as the realm of the ten Buddhas?

Answer: Although the preceding was termed "silence" within the context of names and characteristics, if it pertains to the aspect of fruition (*phala-bhāga*), then from the very beginning, one does not perceive even the slightest trace of name or characteristic.
Question: If that is so, is there no dharma and no entity in this state?
Answer: It is as previously discussed regarding the dharmas in the prior stages; they were non-existent from the very beginning. Question:
In that case, is it truly the case that there is no dharma here?
Answer: It is indeed possessed.
Question: What things are there?
Answer: This is what the ancient masters called the "reversal of emotional views."
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) has the meaning of "carrying.
Question: Since the preceding word already contains three meanings, does "vehicle" likewise possess them?
The answer is as follows:
The meaning of the "vehicle" (*yāna*) of the Three Vehicles refers to that which proceeds from a cause of a different fruit to a fruit of a different cause.
Now, it is designated as "carrying across" (*vāhana*) based on the principle that the cause is itself the fruit.
This is the section on Samantabhadra’s teaching.
It turns its back on the names and characteristics of cause and effect,
based on the meaning of the cessation of the path of speech and the extinction of the sphere of mental activity.
This refers to the meaning of the Samantabhadra’s realization-stage of transport;
as for the fruition-stage of the ocean of nature, it is ineffable,
and thus is described solely as the "inconceivable vehicle."
This refers to the "vehicle" (yāna) by way of being immovable.
There are three meanings of "dharma":
first, its own essence is called dharma.
According to the Three Vehicles,
it is said that outside the self-substance of an ox there is a horse,
and within the self-substance of a horse there is an ox.
Regarding the One Vehicle, it is said:
"Because this dharma does not exist on the side of that dharma,
and that dharma does not exist on the side of this dharma, it is called 'self-substance' (*svabhāva*)."
The second [category] is called "dharmas" (dharma) as the object of the mind.
According to the three vehicles,
that which is confronted by the sixth consciousness is termed the "dharma-object" (dharmāyatana).
According to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna),
that which is confronted by the inexhaustible mental consciousness is termed "Dharma.
The meaning of the three tracks (triyāna) can thus be understood.
The realm (*dhātu*) also has three meanings.
First, the meaning of distinct natures (*gotra*).
This refers to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
This is because the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are distinct from one another.
However, according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), within these three natures, any one may be cited as encompassing the whole, for they are mutually inclusive without partiality;
thus, they are said to be "distinct in nature."
Regarding the meaning of the two causes,
it is said from the perspective of the three vehicles:
only that which gives rise to visual consciousness is called "visual consciousness."

Regarding the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vikalpa-bīja*): from the perspective of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), they universally give rise to the six consciousnesses; thus, they are the seeds of names and phrases for the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Second is the meaning of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*). Regarding the three vehicles,
it means that the cause of a distinct fruit sustains the fruit of a distinct cause.
In terms of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), it is called "sustaining" because the cause that encompasses the entirety of the fruit sustains the fruit that encompasses the entirety of the cause.

As for the diagram, it relies on the image of the Ocean Seal (Sāgaramudrā) to represent the teachings of the One Vehicle and Three Vehicles, as well as the faculties and inclinations [of sentient beings].
That which refers to the distinction between before and after the vermilion seal is the teaching of the Three Vehicles.
The circularity of the vermilion seal is the teaching of the One Vehicle.
The characters within the seal that distinguish its preceding and succeeding parts represent the faculties and inclinations of the three vehicles;
the characters within the seal’s perfection represent the vessel of the one vehicle.
Fǎróng’s *Dèjì* states: "Regarding 'the poem and the seal combined':
a single vermilion line forms the seal by uniting all the black characters; because it completes the circular seal, it is called 'the poem and the seal combined.'"
Question: Do you write the black characters first and then draw the vermilion lines, or do you draw the vermilion lines first and then write the black characters?
Answer: Both methods are correct.
To write first and then draw signifies acting according to principle;
to draw first and then write signifies...
This is the principle of following the phenomenon to realize the underlying truth.
Although Master Yan composed seventy-three mudrās,
he intended them merely to manifest the meaning of a single mudrā.
Because Master Xiang had deeply grasped the Master’s intent,
he performed only this single root mudrā. Zhenxiu Deji says:
As for "poetry" (shi), it refers to a composition of thirty seven-character lines; thus it is called poetry.
It does not refer to speech constrained by rhyme.
Regarding the "single seal":
This is because he wished to manifest a single great dependent origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The *Daji* (Great Record) states:
"As for the fifty-four corners..."
The subsequent text states:
"For what reason does the seal pattern consist of only a single line?
It answers: "It signifies the single voice of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Taking the ten kinds of sounds from the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" and correlating them with the capacities of the five vehicles results in fifty.
This [deity] is able to respond to the Buddha because it fully possesses the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*);
thus, it is called the "four corners. *Zhēnxiù jì* states:
The fifty-four corners represent human knowledge,
namely the fifty-five types of knowledge.
Because the first and last Mañjuśrīs are combined, there are only fifty-four [deities].
By combining the mention of the first and last, the intermediate ones are collectively taken as one Perfect Wisdom (pariniṣpanna-jñāna).
Samantabhadra, the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), is the principle to be realized.
This is because all phenomena within the dharma-realm do not transcend the principle of wisdom.
As for the two hundred and ten characters,
they represent the consciousness of the dharma.
This refers to the two hundred questions on the "Universal Compassion Cloud Arising" from the *Lokottara-parivarta*,
and the two thousand answers from the "Vajra-vessel of Samantabhadra. For each question:
All are answered with ten phrases;
hence it is called "one ten.
The *Daji* (Great Record) states:
The one hundred and ten characters refer to the five cycles of cause and effect.
Excluding the initial cycle of cause and effect, the subsequent four cycles are distinguished by selecting the causes while omitting the effects.
Since there are fifty positions for each of the four surrounding directions,
they total two hundred. Among these,
all the fruition stages (phala-avasthā) within the four directions are combined into one.
Because one wishes to manifest that these fruits are identical to the fruits of the ten Buddhas, it is said "one ten.
Question: Why are the first cause and fruit excluded?
Answer: Because these are merely objects of faith and not practices to be accomplished.
Question: For what reason are they combined into one at the stage of fruition?
Answer: Because there are distinctions at the causal stage.
Because they are equally distinguished by their defining characteristics,
the fruits should likewise be so;
however, because one wishes to manifest that these are all the fruit of the ten Buddhas, they are collectively treated as one.
It is further stated:
"These are the ten gates and ten dharmas of the three worlds manifested within this Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā).
That is to say, the ten coins metaphor from the passage below and the ten universal virtues (daśa-pāramitā) constitute twenty."
The twenty individual treatises each contain ten mysteries,
totaling two hundred;
when combined with the original ten mysteries, they are said to be two hundred and ten.
Furthermore, this mudrā serves as the general [category],
while the seventy-three mudrās serve as the specific ones.
Within these specific mudrās:
The seventy seals are sequentially applied across the three periods;
as there are seventy seals for each period, they total two hundred and ten.
Thus, these two hundred and ten seals combine to form the general characteristic seal of the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
Regarding the thirty seven-character verses:
the preceding ten dharma-analogies,
combined with the ten fundamental mysteries, constitute the thirty.
Since these thirty phrases do not exceed the seven characters of the scripture’s title,
they are composed in heptasyllabic verse. Therefore,
although the dharmas of the dharma-realm are said to be inexhaustible, [they are encompassed herein].
It does not exceed two hundred and ten characters;
taken together, these constitute thirty phrases.
Furthermore, taken as a whole, this does not exceed seven characters.
Furthermore, all of this does not transcend wisdom and reality;
moreover, all of this does not transcend the single most pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Therefore, the title is called "The Diagram of the Dharma-Realm of the One Vehicle."
In the *Qingliang shu* (Commentary by Qingliang), within the general explanation of the title, it says:
"The sixth fascicle 'comprehensively exhausting the characteristics' means that from the subsequent [sections] one gradually rolls them up, until not even the nine assemblies are excluded."
The nine assemblies do not depart from the first assembly;
the first assembly does not depart from the general title;
and the general title does not transcend principle and wisdom.
What is irrational is not wisdom;
therefore, there is no wisdom outside of principle.
What is not wisdom is not principle.
Therefore, since there is no principle external to wisdom,
principle and wisdom are non-dual; furthermore,
wisdom is subsumed within principle.
When separated from the essence, there is no function;
when functions are subsumed back into the essence,
the nature of that essence is itself detached.
Therefore, its essence is non-essence;
it is primordially pure.
It is conventionally designated as the "Pure Dharma-realm."
Therefore, from the ultimate following of the inexhaustible down to a single character or no character,
all are subsumed within the Flower Adornment Ocean of Nature without exception.
The Great Sage’s excellent teachings extend to the various treatments for different ailments.
*Fayong’s Record* states:
"The Great Sage..."
This is because, among all the teachings, this current Teacher is the most honored and supreme.
Question: Is it the case that, within the four lower teachings, both the transformers (the teachers) and the transformed (the disciples) are inferior?

Within the one, all exist; within the many, there is the one.
The *Dharmalakṣaṇa-śāstra* states:
Question: Why is it that, rather than explaining the principle of "not maintaining its own nature but following conditions" first, this phrase is explained next?
Answer: Generally, in the dharma of dependent origination, there is no distinct self-nature;
they mutually take one another as their self-nature.
Only then can it arise in accordance with conditions without partiality.
Therefore, following the explanation that [the dharmadhātu] does not abide in its own nature, this clarifies the meaning of "all within one" and so forth.
Question: If dharmas arising through dependent origination arise in accordance with conditions without partiality, [how is this so?]
Is it solely the meaning of taking as an object that which did not previously exist?
Answer: Speaking in terms of objects, it takes as its object that which did not previously exist.
Discussing this in terms of its nature:
what is it that serves as the preceding condition for dharmas?
When discussing conditions,
the five feet currently appearing within the conditions stand as the fundamental dharma of dependent origination without any lateral deviation; therefore,
prior to these conditions, there is not a single dharma.
When discussing from the perspective of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), it is the originally existent essence of the manifestation of nature (*xingqi*).
As the *Zhenji* states:
The second line, "In one, all are equal," reappears to clarify the meaning of the principle of dependent origination as the manifestation of the essence through conditions.
The first line is the gate of the principle of cause and effect.
That is to say, by attaining one, one necessarily attains ten;
by attaining ten, one necessarily attains one.
By attaining the cause, one immediately attains the fruit.
To attain the fruit is precisely to attain the cause.
The ten conditions are the cause;
that which is accomplished by them is the single fruit.
This principle of cause and effect refers to the immobility of two positions within a single moment;
hence it is called the "Gate of the Principle of Cause and Effect.
The next phrase is the "Gate of Sovereign Virtuous Function."
This means that this is precisely that, and that is precisely this;
there is no obstruction and no partiality.
Therefore, it is called the Gate of Sovereign Virtuous Function and the Gate of the Movement of Positions.
Question: Since the previous section was the "Gate of Power and Lack of Power," whereas this is the "Gate of Essence and Non-Essence," why speak of "function" (yòng)?
Answer: This refers to the meaning that the very essence of causes and conditions is simultaneously cause and effect; it is precisely this that is called "function."
It is not the function of a functional power.
Regarding the question of "all within one," the ten conditions are the causes.
That which is produced is one fruit.
If that is so, does it follow that the combination of the productive cause and the produced result constitutes eleven?
The answer is: within a single condition, it is designated as a "productive cause" in relation to its counterpart.
The meaning of "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*) constitutes the fruit that is realized.
However, because these two meanings are non-dual, they do not constitute eleven [categories].
The *Daji* (Great Record) states:

Within one, all is contained; below, the desire to manifest the principle of cause and effect within the great dependent origination, as well as the meaning of mastery over its virtues and functions, is intended.
Therefore, these two phrases exist.
Master Chongye said:
"The three vehicles also possess this principle.

This means that, according to the Initial Teaching, the seeds of the three natures within the *ālayavijñāna* are of the same indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) as the essence of the fundamental consciousness."
The commentary explains:
The meaning of being perfumed within the substance of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the "substance gate" (*tīmen*).
Furthermore, it is the meaning of the sovereign functioning of its qualities and activities.
The seeds of the three natures (trisvabhāva) according to their respective perfuming agents refer to the gate of power;
this is the meaning of the principle of cause and effect.
In the mature teachings, the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* refers to the meaning of the mastery of virtuous functions.
"Arising and ceasing" refers to the principle of the causal relationship through the functioning [of phenomena].
Since causes are distinguished according to the dharmas within the One Vehicle,
among the ten universal dharmas (daśa-pāramitā-dharma), any single dharma may be cited as embodying both the essence and the function.
As for its essence, it is the sovereign freedom of virtuous function;
as for its function, it is the principle of cause and effect.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Dharma-body":
Question: The waves of the west wind are not the waves of the east wind, and the waves of the east wind are not the waves of the west wind.
Nevertheless, based on the principle that the substance of the water of these two waves is non-dual, one may speak of them as being "identical" (the gate of identity).
If one restricts oneself to two phenomena, one cannot speak of the gate of identity (*ekatva-mukha*).
If that is so, then by restricting oneself to this phenomenon and that phenomenon, since their underlying reality (*tattva*) is non-dual, one may speak of the gate of identity;
why then could one not discuss the gate of identity between these two phenomena without excluding them?
Answer: If one releases two [substances], such as water and wind, there are no two distinct waves.
Since there are no two distinct waves, by means of what could anything be identified as what?
Since this is already identical to that,
one can know that it is the two waves themselves that are discussed as being mutually identical;
it is not a case of mutual identity being discussed in terms of the essence of the principle.
In this context, the water of this wave and the water of that wave are identical in essence.
Therefore, although waves are inexhaustible, the statement that their essence is one refers only to the meaning of the Three Vehicles.
If this wave does not exist, then that wave does not exist;
if that wave does not exist, then this wave does not exist.
This is the middle gate.
Because this wave lacks intrinsic nature, it resides within that wave;
because that wave lacks intrinsic nature, it resides within this wave.
This very gateway is the One Vehicle.
An ancient record states:
Regarding the entry into the inner sanctuary, various schools have established different names;
some, for instance, refer to it as the "Middle Gate" (chūmon) or the "Immediate Gate" (sokumon).
Some say they mutually enter and mutually identify;
some say they mutually abide and mutually are;
others say they mutually assist and mutually encompass.
Some say it is the meaning of the power and lack of power of mutual support;
others say it is the meaning of the presence and absence of essence through mutual negation.
Furthermore, an ancient said:
The middle gates are like the lights of lamps entering one another;
thus, it is simply the functions of the various lamps that enter one another.
Furthermore, the gates are like waves and water mutually containing one another.
Therefore, the substance of the wave and the substance of the water do not possess a single identical characteristic.
This applies likewise from a single atom up to [the vastest scale].
The *Faji* (Record of the Dharma) states:
Regarding "minute particles" (*paramāṇu*):
the initial teaching states they are "extreme minute particles."
The Mature Teaching (Shujiao) says:
"Empty and adjacent to the dust.
The One Vehicle (Ichijō) says: [as above].
The universal characteristic of objects.
As for this universal characteristic of objects:
when it must be small, it is small.
Since the great is immediately the great, the ten directions are manifested instantaneously within a single atom.
Question: What is the difference between the atoms with spatial divisions found in the lower teachings and the atoms of the One Vehicle?
Answer: If one requires that a single atom possess spatial parts, then it possesses spatial parts;
if one requires that it lack spatial parts, then it lacks spatial parts.
They are distinguished because they follow whatever one requires with sovereign ease.
Question: Is it not the case that particles which lack spatial parts cannot be further fragmented?
Answer: They too must be reduced to their ultimate limit. Why is this so?
If one’s intention is to maintain that what is being reckoned has no spatial divisions, then it is necessary to employ the analysis of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).
The *Zhēnjì* states:
"Within a single atom, the ten directions are contained."
Is it because the realms of the ten directions are subsumed into a single atom that it is said to "contain the ten directions"?
Or, once the realms of the ten directions have been gathered into a single atom, does this newly formed atom further contain the ten directions?
Answer: Both meanings are tenable.
Question: When a single atom is formed, it encompasses all of the ten directions without remainder;
how, then, can it newly contain [all things] anew?
Answer: Because it is necessary where it is necessary.
When a single atom is formed, it must be necessary for all ten directions, and it must newly and freshly contain time.
Nor does it obstruct subsequent occurrences.
The *Mahā-vyutpatti* states: "A single atom."
Because it has been refined through diligent cultivation throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field,
one is finally able to contain the worlds of the ten directions with unimpeded mastery.
This is the most subtle initial stage of the phenomena of the phenomenal realm (*vastu-dharma*).
The "Cloud of True Samādhi Virtue" states:
"As for the gate of phenomena merging to manifest principle,
this refers merely to the principle that objects contain the ten directions."
This does not mean that a single speck of dust is extinguished and merged into the same principle.
The "Chapter on the Dharma-body" states: Master Xiang said:
As for the fact that a single atom contains the worlds of the ten directions,
it is so because they are equally without abiding.
The Master Yuan asked:
Question: Is the infinitesimal atom "non-abiding smallness," while the worlds of the ten directions are "non-abiding greatness"?
Answer: They are of one measure.
Question: If that is so, why say that the atom is small while the worlds of the ten directions are vast?
Answer: The atom and the worlds of the ten directions each lack intrinsic nature; they are simply non-abiding.
Regarding what was said about the "small" dust-motes and the "large" world-systems:
these are designated as such because they are required for the purpose at hand;
it is not that they are small that they are called "small," nor is it that they are large that they are called "large."
This means that because sentient beings do not know that the small particles within the great world-system are vast,
one speaks of the small particles as being large within the world-system; it does not mean,
however, that the small nature of the particles and the large nature of the world-system are unilaterally fixed as their respective intrinsic natures.
It may also be said that the world is large while the dust mote is small;
in principle, they are equal, being the non-abiding true reality (*dharmatā*).
An ancient record states:
There are particles that are increasingly minute and small;
there are particles that are increasingly vast and large;
and there are particles that remain as minute as they originally were.
The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:
"The atom, the minute particle, gold-dust, water-dust,
rabbit-dust, sheep-dust, cow-dust, and mote-dust."

The nit, the louse, the barley grain, and the finger-joint each increase sevenfold over the preceding one. As for the "dust mote" (tiraṇīka): [it is the dust particle seen in a sunbeam entering through a crack].
The dust motes seen by the human eye are those that move within the sunlight streaming through a window crack.
When these are divided into seven parts, what is seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is one-seventh of that part.
These two types of dust—the mote seen through a window crack and its seventh part—are the aforementioned dusts.
Dividing that which is seen by the divine eye into seven parts, one such part is an iron atom (*loharaja*);
this is what is seen by those in the first fruit (*prathamaphala*). Dividing that into seven parts, one such part is a copper atom (*tāmrajasa*).
The second fruit perceives this [silver particle] analyzed down to one-seventh of a silver mote (*rajaparamāṇu*).
The third fruit perceives it [further].
Dividing this further until one-seventh of a *suvarṇa-rajas* (gold-dust) is reached is what is seen by those in the fourth fruit (*caturtha-phala*).
Dividing this further until one-seventh of a *ab-rajas* (water-dust) is reached is [the object of the next stage].
It is what is seen by a Great Pratyekabuddha;
it is what is seen by a Buddha who, having analyzed this [atom] down to one-seventh of a subtle particle,
attains enlightenment by severing the fetters in thirty-four moments of thought.
The commentary states:
All of the above are subsumed under the category of the parikalpita (imagined nature).
When these are analyzed down to a single ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), which is one-seventh of a [visible] dust mote, [they are no longer perceived].
This is what is seen by a bodhisattva at the initial stage of instruction;
it is analyzed down to one-seventh of a minute particle (*paramāṇu*).
This is what is seen by the Buddha of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*).
The commentary states:
This is subsumed under the aforementioned dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
When this is analyzed down to its seventh constituent, it is a single factor within the category of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This is what the Buddha perceives according to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*):
by analyzing [matter] down to one-seventh of a particle of emptiness (*śūnya-rajas*).
This is what the Buddha perceives according to the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-naya*).
The commentary states:
From the Final Teaching (Jiao) onward, these are subsumed under the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Within this context, both the dharmas of form and mind are constituted by True Suchness (tathatā).
This final teaching states that the objects of the sense-fields are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The initial teaching also speaks of the objects of the mental consciousness;
however, within the final teaching, a single mental consciousness is established.
Therefore, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that which is seen by the eye of the single mind constitutes the object-field of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*).
When this is analyzed down to one-seventh of its total characteristics,
it becomes the object-field of Samantabhadra’s eye.
The objects perceived by this Universal Eye cannot be seen by the five eyes of the three vehicles;
therefore, this sutra seeks to demonstrate the meaning of the unique, distinct teaching.
Taking the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) and empty space as the primary stage.
Question: What is the difference between this atom of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the principle (*tattva*) of the Three Vehicles?
Answer: From the perspective of the Three Vehicles, it is said that this is precisely that principle.
From the perspective of what is seen by the Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus), this refers to the most subtle phenomena (*dharmas*).
Although the preceding explanation initially cites the *Abhidharmakośa*,
it does not actually represent the tenets of that treatise.
This is the meaning bestowed by Linde upon Rongxiu;
it is explained in accordance with the sacred teachings regarding the essence of contemplation of the mind.
Furthermore, the Record states:
The seven subtle particles are:
the mote floating in a window,
and the wool-fiber dust.
A rabbit-hair mote,
a cow-hair mote,
and a gold-dust mote.
"Water-dust" refers to the *paramāṇu* (extremely subtle atom).
The commentary explains:
"Window-dust" refers to dust floating in the sunlight through a window crack.
"Wool-fiber dust" refers to...
Because a mote of dust moving in a window-opening is divided into seven parts,
it is merely the tip of a wool-fiber.
As for a rabbit-hair mote:
Because a wool-dust particle is divided into seven parts,
one does not stop at the wool-dust but proceeds to the tip of a rabbit-hair dust particle.
As for the cow-hair dust particle:
By dividing a rabbit-hair mote into seven parts,
one reaches the limit of the tip of a cow's belly hair;
by dividing this into seven parts, it passes through gold and emerges from it without being obstructed.
To divide this into seven means that water cannot moisten it;
to divide this into seven refers to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Because each of these individual particles gives rise to [a further particle], they are called "seven-mother atoms" (*sapta-mātṛka-rajas*).
These extremely subtle atoms are divided and analyzed into three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) within the Initial Teaching;
based on these atoms of the Initial Teaching,
they are further divided and analyzed into uncountable eons within the Final Teaching.
Within the One Vehicle, one may divide and analyze it across kalpas as numerous as the atoms of two Buddha-worlds;
only upon reaching the ultimate limit of subtlety does it become a single atom of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the statement that "immeasurable distant kalpas are identical to a single thought-moment," it is recorded that this refers to the formation of dharmas through the process of separation over immeasurable and distant kalpas.
He vertically splits a single hair into ten parts, and even into a hundred or a thousand parts;
he places one of these parts upon a jade plate and severs it with a sharp blade.
The moment when the sharp edge of the blade reaches the board is defined as one thought-moment (*ekacitta*).
The *Shinjiki* states:
"As for 'ten ages'..."
One interpretation says it refers to the tenth world,
because it is a mindfulness of the general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). Another interpretation says it refers to the ten worlds.
This is because they are presented both collectively and individually.

Question: If the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) takes a single moment of the present as its temporal period, is it the case that the temporal periods of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) consist solely of these eight?
Answer: With reference to a single present moment,
when compared to the past and future of that same present,
they are established as distinct characteristics based on their mutual relation as preceding and succeeding.
Therefore, the world of distinct characteristics consists of nine and not eight;
yet, when one does not look to what precedes or follows but rather encompasses all through absolute transcendence,
it constitutes the tenth world of universal characteristics.
The *Dajiji* (Great Record) states:
"Does the ninth world immediately enter to constitute the tenth world?
Or is it that one further discusses 'immediate entry' with respect to the tenth world?"
Answer: Both meanings are valid.
Thus, K'ang-tsang said:
"However, because these nine time-periods mutually interpenetrate one another, they form a single comprehensive statement."
The general and the particular together constitute the ten periods of time (*daśakāla*).
Because these ten periods are fully endowed with distinctness while simultaneously manifesting as mutual conditions, they achieve mutual interpenetration (*anyonya-anupraveśa*).
To explain:
The first explanation [of the nine periods] involves their mutual inclusion to form the tenth period;
the latter explanation concerns the ten periods, causing them to mutually include one another.
The *Zhiguān zhǐguī yuántōng chāo* states:
In the Three Vehicles, because the establishment of dharmas is solitary, time is separated from the dharma;
since the dharma itself is subject to flux, time also flows.
In the One Vehicle, because the establishment of dharmas is complete, time is separated from the dharma.
Because phenomena do not transmigrate, time does not transmigrate.
Thus, the *Sūtra of the Necklace* (*Śrīkaṇṭhaka-sūtra*) states that the Buddha told King Brahmadatta:
"That dog lying before you was your body in a past life;
my stroking you is your future Buddhahood," and so forth.
Furthermore, the monk Zhītōng of Luóguó was one of the ten holy disciples of Master Xiāng.
Dwelling at Miri Rock Cave on Mount Daebak, he practiced the contemplation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One day, he suddenly saw a large boar pass by the entrance of his cave.
Upon seeing it, he followed his usual practice of fashioning a wooden image of the Honored One, performing every rite with the utmost sincerity.
The speaking image replied:
"The pig that passed through the hole was your body in a past life;
I am the Buddha who is your future fruition."
Upon hearing these words, Tong immediately realized the principle that the three periods of time are of a single limit.
Later, he went to see Master Xiang to discuss this;
the Master recognized that he had become a vessel for the Dharma.
He then conferred upon him the seal of the Dharma-realm diagram (*dharmadhātu-maṇḍala*). Thus far,

although there are differences in time regarding the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, and distinctions between the central and peripheral regions, [the account] is consistent with the history of King Brahmadatta.
However, their causes and conditions are likewise similar, and so forth.
Within the Three Vehicles, in the past there was only the state of a dog;
in the present, there is only the state of a human.
In the future, it exists only at the stage of Buddhahood.
Thus, one proceeds from a past dog to a present human,
and from a present human to a future Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that because the establishment of the Dharma within the Three Vehicles is solitary, the Dharma is separated from time;
for the Dharma is impermanent,
and time is likewise impermanent.
Within the One Vehicle, the past dog-vehicle contains the human-Buddha;
the present human-vehicle contains the dog-Buddha;
and within the future Buddha-vehicle, the dog-human is contained.
Therefore, one does not transmigrate from a past dog into a present human, nor does one transition from a present human into a future Buddha.
Thus it is said that within the One Vehicle, phenomena are established such that they interpenetrate; consequently, although time is separated, the Dharma is not.
Since dharmas are eternally abiding, time is also eternally abiding.
Question: Although dharmas are one, do they mutually constitute nine periods of time?
If it is asked whether the nine temporal distinctions of phenomena are themselves distinct,
the answer is as stated in the subsequent explanation;
that is, taking my own person as an illustration.
Approximating by month within a year, there are twelve months in a year; therefore, my body also consists of twelve parts.
Since one month has thirty days, the body also consists of thirty parts.
Since there are twelve periods in a day, the body likewise has twelve parts.
Since there are eight *ke* in one period, the body likewise has eight parts.
Thus, because there are three hundred and sixty days in a year and one hundred *ke* in a day, the body likewise has thirty-six thousand parts.
Therefore, just as the nine periods are distinct, the dharmas within them are also distinct.
Question: Regarding the discussion of the nine periods based on the five positions:
yesterday was the past of the past, and thus it is only one.
Regarding yesterday, if one considers its own essence, it is both past and present;
yet in relation to today, it is both present and past.
Therefore, it possesses both aspects.
Today, when viewed in relation to yesterday, is past and future;
with respect to its own essence, it is present;
and when viewed in relation to tomorrow, it is future and past.
Therefore, all three [time periods] are complete.
From the perspective of looking back from tomorrow to today, it is the present and the future;
yet, in terms of their own essential nature, they are the future and the present.
Therefore, it possesses both [past and future aspects]. Since "tomorrow" is the future, and the future is singular,
it is thus solely through the mutual observation of the five positions that the nine times are established.
Thus, dharmas are indeed only one;
yet, because they are discussed in relation to one another, they also constitute the nine temporal states of dharmas.
Why, then, do you say that just as the nine temporal states are distinct, the dharmas themselves must also be distinct?
The answer to Kangzang is as follows:
It is known to be so because time and phenomena are inseparable.
Within the Three Vehicles, form, mind, and so forth are phenomena.
Based on the meaning of the prior and posterior flux of these phenomena, "time" is established;
therefore, time is merely a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*).
For this reason, we shall not discuss this matter further.
Within the One Vehicle, because time and phenomena are inseparable,
time is also real. Therefore,
just as there are distinctions in time, so too are there distinctions in phenomena.
The "Chapter on the Dharma-body" states:
"It is like a single night of dreaming;
there are three [periods] for the father already passed and three for the son yet to be born, totaling nine."
When perceived during the waking state,
it exists solely within a single thought-moment;
it is not that a fragment of this mind is divided to become the father.
One part is divided for myself;
one part is divided for my son;
both are contained within a single mind.
Whatever is mentioned is immediately subsumed;
although these nine persons have no mutual cognition of one another,
it is not that the distinction between the nine persons is entirely absent.
Furthermore, it is not that three are established as existent and six are established as nonexistent outside of a single thought-moment;
existence and nonexistence coexist within a single thought-moment, and there is no distinction between existence and nonexistence. The above is concluded.
Therefore, because that very mind of non-self-retribution is entirely the father, entirely the self, and entirely the son,
it is distinct just as the nine temporal dharmas are distinct.

Question: What is the difference between the specific meaning of distinguishing the present single moment from the other eight periods of time, and the general meaning of impartially encompassing all within the nine periods?
Answer: Master Yan used an analogy to show this to Master Xiang, saying: [text follows].
It is like a man who dreams that his father and grandfather have climbed onto a roof with a covering,
while his son and grandson are below handing up the tiles;
he himself stands in between, passing them down in succession.
The grandfather is past;
being past, he occupies only one position.
The father is both past and present.
Because it possesses both the past and the present, it is endowed with two positions.
The intermediate body, however, is past, future, and present; because it possesses the present, the future, and the past, it is endowed with three positions.
The son belongs to both positions because he is both present and future, as well as future and present;
the grandson belongs to only one position because he is solely future.
As for the person who transmits the tile in the interim, if one considers his actual status, he is distinguished from the other eight generations.
Therefore, the present is indeed the present.
As for the five people who appeared in the dream, they do not correspond exclusively to any single one among the nine periods of time.
Thus, this person possesses both meanings mentioned above.
Therefore, this is the method of separating the general and the specific by means of time.
The "Chapter on the Body of the Path" states:
"Ten days before Master Yan’s spirit departed."
The disciples came forward to offer their greetings.
The Master asked the assembly:
"In the sutras, it is said that within a single atom are contained the worlds of the ten directions, and that immeasurable eons are equal to a single thought-moment."
"What do you see? they asked. The assembly replied, "It is because the dharmas of dependent origination lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
the small does not abide in the small, the large does not abide in the large, the short does not abide in the short, and the long does not abide in the long; is it for this reason?"
The Master said, “It is indeed so, it is indeed so.
Yet you still say, ‘How is it that there is still birth? The Master said:
Do not speak too much;
simply state that it is because of one reason:
from the initial generation of the mind until the time of eternal harmony.
The *Faji* (Record of the Dharma) states:

Question: Why is it that, following the sequence in which the nine periods and ten periods are mutually identical, the principle that "at the very moment of first generating the resolve, one attains perfect enlightenment" is taught?
Answer: Because the dharmas of the stage of realization (*pramāṇa-bhāga*) cannot be apprehended.
Because there may be practitioners who have no share in this,
for their sake it is shown by means of the dharma-nature of the "share of realization" (pratyātmavedya-dharmatā), saying:
"First, there is no intrinsic nature, for all things have [this] as their nature."
A single atom has no self-nature, for its nature is the ten directions.
Incalculable eons have no self-nature, for their nature is a single thought-moment.
A single thought-moment has no self-nature, for its nature is incalculable eons.
This is what is called the profound true nature (*tathatā*).
The practitioner thinks:
"I have already known the true nature; how can it be realized?"
Therefore, he further instructed:
"One must certainly take this true nature as the mind from which one sets forth.
Thereupon, the practitioner sets forth in this manner.
Therefore, the very arousal of the mind is itself the fulfillment of the fruit.
For this reason, when abiding in nirvāṇa, one constantly wanders through saṃsāra;
and when wandering through saṃsāra, one constantly abides in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are always in harmony.
The passage on the Buddha-nature (*buddhagotra*) in the *Xuánshì zhāng* states:
"The third [section], concerning the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), has two explanations."
First, it subsumes the various teachings elucidated in the preceding sections;
all are fully present as primary and attendant elements to constitute the school,
because they belong to the same teaching.
Because it encompasses skillful means;
second, because according to the distinct teaching of the spiritual lineage (gotra),
the profound cause and fruit are non-dual.
It encompasses both the basis and the correct [path],
exhausting the three worlds and including everything therein.
Because the various dharma-gates of understanding the principle and practicing the phenomena have been primordially fulfilled and already matured,
the Great Sūtra states:
"The bodhisattva lineage is profoundly deep and vast, equal to the dharma-dhātu and space."
This is what is meant by that. The *Zhēnjì* (True Record) states:
"At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one is already a perfectly awakened one."
According to the provisional teaching (samaya-samvṛti),
it is said that within the stages of the three worthies and ten grounds, the initial stage of the ten understandings— the first dwelling of the resolve for awakening—
is perfected; furthermore, the Buddha perfects the dwellings such as the "dwelling of cultivating the ground" and so forth.
The Buddha’s manifestation of these differences in the obscurity of ignorance is merely a provisional display.
According to the Separate Teaching (biejiao),

yet it arises according to the number of sentient beings.

because space is limitless, worlds are limitless; because worlds are limitless, sentient beings are limitless.
Within these limitless sentient beings...

The *Zhenji* states:

therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
